name: Chullachaqui
description: The Chullachaqui (Quechua chulla 'odd / unequal' + chaki 'foot') is a forest spirit of Peruvian and Brazilian Amazonia, depicted as a small humanoid with one mismatched foot — typically one human foot and one animal hoof — who shapeshifts into a familiar person to lead unwary travellers astray.
full_description: The Chullachaqui (also spelled Chullachaki, Shapingo, or in Brazilian Portuguese Curupira) is one of the most widespread forest spirits of the Western Amazon basin, attested in Quechua, Cocama-Cocamilla, Shipibo-Conibo, Yagua, and mestizo riverine traditions of Peru, eastern Ecuador, and adjoining Brazilian Amazonia. The figure is consistently described as a small (roughly one-metre) male humanoid with one foot conspicuously different from the other — usually one human foot and one animal foot (a deer, peccary, jaguar, tapir, or rooster), in some versions reversed or twisted. The Chullachaqui's central narrative function is shapeshifting: it appears in the form of a relative, friend, or trusted local in order to lure a victim deep into the forest, then reveals its true nature and leaves the person hopelessly disoriented, sometimes for days. The mismatched foot is the only sure way to detect the deception, since the spirit cannot disguise its footprints. Beyond pranks, the Chullachaqui is widely understood as a guardian (dueño) of the forest, its plants, and its game animals; respectful behaviour, ritual offerings (typically of mapacho tobacco) and an apology before hunting are traditional means of avoiding its anger. Modern Amazonian shamanism, particularly the ayahuasca traditions of Loreto and Ucayali, integrates the Chullachaqui into its cosmology as a powerful but dangerous spirit teacher; eco-tourism and contemporary literature have also adopted it as a symbol of Amazonian conservation.

aliases.name: Curupira
aliases.meaning: Closely related Tupi-Guarani forest spirit, sometimes equated with the Chullachaqui

aliases.name: Shapingo
aliases.meaning: Local variant name in mestizo folklore

origin: Western Amazon basin: lowland Peru (especially Loreto, Ucayali, San Martín, and Madre de Dios), eastern Ecuador (Pastaza, Napo), western Brazil (Acre, Amazonas), and the headwaters region of Colombia and Bolivia.

etymology.meaning: 'One foot' or 'mismatched foot', referring to its diagnostic feature.
etymology.first_use: Quechua oral tradition predates documented written usage; recorded in Spanish-language Amazonian ethnographic and folkloric collections from the 19th and 20th centuries onward.

timeline.event: Quechua and Amazonian oral traditions of forest-owning spirits include the chulla-chaki figure
Spanish chroniclers in the Andes and Amazon record duendes and forest-spirit traditions among indigenous peoples
timeline.significance: Provides earliest colonial-period framing of Amazonian forest-spirit beliefs (general; the Chullachaqui by name is later)

timeline.event: Peruvian folklorists (e.g. Mario Florián, Arturo Jiménez Borja) and indigenous-language scholars publish accounts of Chullachaqui in collections of Amazonian myth and legend
timeline.significance: Anchors the figure in academic folklore studies

timeline.event: Chullachaqui becomes a routine subject in Amazonian shamanic and ayahuasca-tourism literature, including works by Luis Eduardo Luna and Steve Beyer
timeline.significance: Brings the figure into wider international awareness
timeline.source: Luna, L. E. & Amaringo, P. (1991), Ayahuasca Visions; Beyer, S. (2009), Singing to the Plants

related.name: Curupira
related.description: Brazilian (Tupi-Guarani) forest spirit with backward-pointing feet; closely cognate with the Chullachaqui

related.name: Duende
related.description: Spanish-American small forest/household spirit; shares trickster forest-guardian role

related.name: Patasola
related.description: Colombian one-legged forest spirit who lures men deep into the forest

related.name: La Tunda
related.description: Afro-Colombian forest spirit who shape-shifts into loved ones to lure victims

related.name: El Sisimite
related.description: Central American forest spirit / hairy hominid in shared 'forest abductor' tradition

related.name: Yacuruna
related.description: Aquatic counterpart in Amazonian cosmology; underwater spirits whose terrestrial complement includes the Chullachaqui

cultural_notes: The Chullachaqui is a real being that should be neither sought nor mocked. Hunters and travellers offer mapacho tobacco and ask permission before entering deep forest, and avoid speaking its name unnecessarily.

sources.title: Ayahuasca Visions: The Religious Iconography of a Peruvian Shaman
Singing to the Plants: A Guide to Mestizo Shamanism in the Upper Amazon
The Legend of the Chullachaqui: Myths of the Peruvian Amazon
Spooky Peru: The Myth of the Chullachaqui in the Amazon
